no_evidence_found.nearest_evidence: (1) Zhuang et al. 2023 Front Pharmacol review of Chinese medicine and digoxin (49 articles). Snippets did not show whether sanqi is covered; the full text needs checking (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2023.1040778/full). (2) Dasgupta group: Asian, Siberian and American ginseng (Panax ginseng / P. quinquefolius / Eleutherococcus, not P. notoginseng) interfere with some digoxin immunoassays (FPIA, MEIA, Digoxin III) but not newer chemiluminescent/turbidimetric ones (e.g. PMID 17425395; PMC6649030; PMC6807190). Same genus as sanqi, but notoginseng itself was not tested in what I saw. Do not extrapolate. (3) In vitro: intestinal-bacterial ginsenoside metabolites (CK, PPD, PPT) lowered the digoxin efflux ratio in Caco-2 cells (search summary only; study not identified well enough to cite). (4) A Hello Pharmacist checker says 'no interactions found' but adds this does not mean none exist; not usable as a none_reported source.

no_evidence_found.searched: Web search (snippets only): 'notoginsenoside amlodipine pharmacokinetics rats'; '"notoginseng" "amlodipine" interaction study'; Chinese '三七 OR 血塞通 氨氯地平 药物相互作用 药代动力学'; MSKCC Panax notoginseng page (blocked).
no_evidence_found.nearest_evidence: (1) A Chinese abstract (summarised by search): 5 weeks of IV Panax notoginseng saponin injection in rats showed non-significant trends towards higher AUC and lower clearance of nimodipine (a different calcium channel blocker); the authors suggested possible CYP3A4/2C9/1A2 inhibition. Injection, different drug, non-significant, so not usable. (2) Red ginseng (Panax ginseng, not sanqi) had a negligible pharmacokinetic interaction with amlodipine in rats (PMID 25343287). Different herb. (3) Hello Pharmacist checker: 'no interactions found', with a caveat; not usable.

no_evidence_found.searched: Web search (snippets only): 'Panax notoginseng furosemide OR safflower furosemide interaction'; '"furosemide" "notoginseng" OR "safflower" OR "Carthamus tinctorius" pharmacokinetic interaction'; 'safflower OR notoginseng case report ... hypokalaemia furosemide herbal'.
no_evidence_found.nearest_evidence: Red ginseng (Panax ginseng) raised furosemide Cmax and AUC in horses (Front Vet Sci 2023, PMC10704239). There is also an older case of reduced diuretic response with a ginseng-germanium product, which the authors attributed mainly to germanium. Both concern other herbs/products, not sanqi. Rat CYP studies of notoginseng total saponins plus safflower flavonoids exist (e.g. Biomed Chromatogr 2021, doi 10.1002/bmc.5171), but furosemide is not a CYP-dependent drug and these do not address it.

no_evidence_found.nearest_evidence: (1) Zhuang et al. 2023 Chinese medicine–digoxin review: snippets did not show whether safflower is covered. Check the full text. (2) Hydroxysafflor yellow A altered CYP isozyme activity/expression in rats (PMID 24373810, abstract findings not seen); not about digoxin, which is mainly cleared unchanged. (3) Flos carthami injection inhibited CYP2D6 and slowed metoprolol metabolism in rats (PMC2994065); a different drug. (4) Hello Pharmacist checker: 'no interactions found between Digoxin and Safflower', with a caveat that this does not mean none exist; not usable as a none_reported source.

no_evidence_found.nearest_evidence: No safflower–amlodipine study found. Related: Danshen tablets lowered amlodipine exposure in rats (PMC6507817, already the source for danshen-amlodipine; a different herb). Flos carthami inhibited CYP2D6 in rats (PMC2994065); amlodipine is mainly a CYP3A4 substrate, so this does not apply. A 2014 Chinese review (Chin J Clin Pharmacol Ther 19(6):701) on amlodipine interactions came up in searches, but the snippet did not mention safflower.
